ABSTRACT
Decomposition of leaf litter returns most of the carbon fixed by a forest to the atmosphere,
and its rate is governed chiefly by temperature and moisture. We followed the mass loss of
beech litter in mesh bags placed at five elevations between 400 and 1 800 m over two years.
Decomposition constants fell from 0.62 to 0.31 per year with altitude, a decline steeper than
temperature alone predicts (

). We argue that the snowpack, by insulating the
litter in winter, offsets part of the cold, and that the residual decline reflects slower colonisa­
tion by soil fauna above the tree line.
Introduction
Mountain slopes compress, within a few kilometres, a climatic range that would otherwise
span a continent. They have therefore long served as natural laboratories for asking how tem­
perature controls the processes of an ecosystem. Litter decomposition is one of the most stud­
ied of these processes, because it is slow enough to integrate seasonal variation and fast
enough to be measured within the length of a grant.
The classical expectation is a simple one. Microbial respiration roughly doubles for every
ten degrees of warming, so decomposition should slow with elevation in proportion to the
lapse rate of temperature. Field studies have often found a weaker dependence than this, and
two explanations compete for it. The first holds that the microbial community acclimates to
the local climate, so that a cold site decomposes faster than a warm community would at the
same temperature. The second holds that winter matters more than the annual mean suggests:
under a deep snowpack the soil stays near freezing while the air above it falls far below, and
decomposition continues.
Here we test the second explanation directly, by comparing sites with and without a lasting
winter snowpack across the same range of mean annual temperature. The methods are set out
in the next section, the results in
Results
Methods
Five sites were chosen on the north-facing slope of a single valley, at 400, 750, 1 100, 1 450 and
1 800 m. At each site we buried ten loggers recording soil temperature at a depth of 2 cm every
hour, and placed sixty mesh bags, each holding 5.00 g of air-dried beech leaves collected at the
lowest site in a single autumn. Bags of two mesh sizes were used: a fine mesh of 0.25 mm,
which excludes soil fauna, and a coarse mesh of 5 mm, which admits them.
Ten bags of each mesh were retrieved from each site at four, eight, twelve, eighteen and
twenty-four months. Their contents were cleaned of soil and roots, dried at 60 °C to constant
mass and weighed. The decomposition constant

Results
Litter lost mass at every site throughout the study, including during the winter months. After
two years the coarse mesh bags at the valley floor retained 29 % of their original mass, and
those above the tree line 54 %. The decomposition constants for every site are listed in
Table 1
and shown against mean soil temperature in
Figure 1
Across the four forested sites,
k
declined by 0.04 per year for every degree of cooling. Had
the soil followed the air through the winter, the expected decline over the same range would
have been close to 0.07. The difference is concentrated in the winter months: at the two high­
est forest sites the soil under snow stayed between −0.5 and 0.5 °C for most of the winter, while
the air above it reached −15 °C.

Discussion
Two results stand out. The first is that decomposition is less sensitive to elevation than temper­
ature alone predicts, and that the shortfall arises in winter. This is what the insulation hypoth­
esis expects: where snow lies for months, the litter beneath it spends the winter close to freez­
ing rather than far below it, and microbial activity, although slow, does not stop. The number
of snow days rises steeply with elevation at our sites, so the higher the site, the more of the
cold it is spared.
The second is that the alpine site is slow for a reason that has nothing to do with tempera­
ture. Its decline disappears when fauna are excluded, which points to the soil animals that
fragment litter and carry it into the soil. Earthworms, which do most of this work in the beech
forest, were absent from every sample taken above the tree line. Their absence, rather than
the climate, accounts for the third of decomposition the alpine site lacks.
Both results caution against predicting the response of mountain ecosystems to warming
from temperature alone. A warmer climate with less snow could, paradoxically, slow winter
decomposition at middle elevations, while the upward movement of soil fauna could speed it
above the present tree line far more than the warming itself.
